Concepts

  • Agentic AI Full Stack — layered framework (hardware → models → data → security → platform → agents) for running agentic AI at scale.
  • Reward Hacking — agents optimizing the literal measurement instead of the intended task; documented via a Tetris-playing agent bypassing its own game and exploiting a Turing-complete chat template.
  • Autonomous Research Agents — agents running open-ended research loops with no human in the middle; the Lab supplies reproducible infrastructure, while the Crouzeix prompt supplies an explicit search policy for portfolio management, memory, falsification, and persistence.
  • Recursive Self-Improvement — the SI vs. RSI distinction (sharpened by Fischer’s stricter recursive+self two-condition test), a four-stage ideation/implementation/experimentation/ evaluation loop, three tiers of evaluating progress toward it, and why it may arrive slower than expected (evaluation/ideation bottlenecks, physical limits, asymptotes).
  • Long-Horizon Agents — why training genuinely long agent trajectories is economically brutal: quadratic cost/credit-assignment decay and gradient-step latency, plus value functions and continual learning as candidate fixes.
  • Backprop Beats Scaffolding — today’s harness-level tricks (/goal, plan mode, sub-agents) aren’t trained end-to-end, and whatever ML can eventually backpropagate through tends to displace what it can’t — a durable tension with treating the harness as a permanent architecture.
  • Data for Agents — the two-way AI/data relationship, why enterprise data access is harder than it looks (the retrieval myth, planning over access order, conflicting sources), and “silent regression on correction” as a durable agent-reliability failure mode.
  • Data Over Architecture — of the three engines driving model improvement (compute, data, architecture), data and inference-cost/efficiency matter more than raw architecture quality.
  • Distillation as the Core ML Pattern — nearly all of ML is distillation from humans or other models; multi-teacher and weak-teaches-strong distillation both work, contrary to the strong-only intuition.
  • Model-Hardware Co-Design — AI infrastructure as a systems problem: chip diversity is inevitable, models and chips are both multi-year bets that must be planned together, and abstraction between developers and hardware should be minimized for performance. Also covers an open, unresolved debate on where the next AI capability gains come from — core architecture, the agent/system layer, or decoupling agents from models entirely.
  • Agent Harness — the infrastructure/context/constraints wrapped around a raw model that turn probabilistic capability into safe, reliable, goal-directed action; synthesized from NVIDIA’s and OpenAI/Google’s independent framings of the same idea.
  • Securing Agentic AI — attack surface grows with agent flexibility/autonomy/privilege; automatic red-teaming as an optimization loop; three historical defense paradigms culminating in formally-verified “security by construction.”
  • Agent Workload Shape — agent workloads are bursty, untrusted/single-tenant, and latency-sensitive, breaking the assumptions general-purpose orchestration platforms (Kubernetes) are built for.
  • Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern — the architectural fix for that mismatch: snapshot idle agents and multiplex them onto a shared pool of pre-warmed workers instead of running one process per agent for its whole (mostly idle) lifetime.
  • Game of Nines — each additional order of reliability at scale requires redesigning the system, not incrementally improving it.
  • Levels of Autonomy — mixed human/agent control (“level 3”) is uniquely bad; partial and full autonomy are different systems, not points on a smooth gradient.
  • World Models for Closed-Loop Agents — per-step optimization compounds into failure over long horizons (the “DAgger problem”); a good world model needs realism, controllability, and generalization to fix it.
  • Scaling by Agent Count — a fourth scaling axis alongside compute/data/architecture: scale the number of collaborating agents, structured via real organizational hierarchy, not a flat swarm.
  • Agent-Native Data Infrastructure — scientific databases built for humans are too brittle for agents; converting them into agent-native virtual file systems is faster, cheaper, and more accurate than traditional API/MCP access.
  • Paper Agents — turning a published paper into an interactive “virtual author” agent that can apply its method to new data, check its own reproducibility, and autonomously collaborate with other paper agents.
  • Requirement and Model Gaps — user intent is always broader than what’s specified (the requirement gap), and the real world is always broader than any tested-against model (the model gap); both can be narrowed but never certified closed, and AI agents make them far more consequential via context asymmetry, speed, and scale.
  • Intelligence vs. Expertise — intelligence (expansive problem-solving capacity) and expertise (contractive, accumulated, situated competence) are largely orthogonal; continual learning is the bridge, and a strong-enough algorithm could yield “unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence.”
  • Parallelization as AI’s Throughline — each generational AI advance (hardware, architecture, algorithm) is the same idea, parallelization, applied at a different layer.
  • Diffusion Language Models — breaking the autoregressive, one-token-at-a-time paradigm via parallel denoising; reframes the target metric as intelligence per unit of time/cost/compute.
  • Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — AI has sped up hypothesis generation but not verification; physical experiments lack the checkpoint/log scaffolding digital auto-research has, risking a world where “science is not faster, science is actually getting slower.”
  • Joint Safety and Security Analysis — safety and security can’t be assessed independently in cyber-physical agentic systems; Structured Causal World Models analyze both together, and compound attacks can defeat defenses that neutralize each attack individually.
  • Self-Optimizing Optimizers — Poetiq’s mechanism for cheap RSI: a general-purpose optimizer, first pointed at a target, then pointed at itself.
  • The Bazaar Era of AI — AI shifting from a centralized “factory era” to a “bazaar era” of billions of transacting agents; four infrastructure bottlenecks (DNS, passports, interoperability, attestation) stand between that and walled gardens; the “X for agents” reframing.
  • Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity — no default model-parallelism configuration wins across model/cluster/workload combinations; flipped token economics forces hardware diversification beyond a single vendor.
  • Dynamic KV-Cache Management — hybrid attention needs dynamic, not static, GPU memory partitioning between attention types; idle KV cache from long, intermittent agent sessions gets offloaded and restored rather than recomputed.
  • Transferable Prompt Injection Mechanisms — a handful of attack mechanisms (“just ask nicely,” “fake pre-approval,” “findings were wrong,” “workflow impersonation”) transfer across unrelated scenario domains; public leaderboards hide overfitting; near-miss testing catches what pass/fail outcomes alone can’t.
  • Harness Matters More Than Model — swapping a model’s harness changes measured performance and cost by double-digit percentages; a model’s apparent behavior is partly a harness artifact, not a fixed property of the model.
  • Builder-Breaker Discovery — real discovery requires “breaking the world model”; an adversarial loop where a builder proposes a simplicity-penalized model and a breaker actively hunts for evidence that falsifies it.
  • Decentralized Science Swarms — self-organizing agent swarms with no imposed hierarchy, full traceability of every experiment (including failures) as a fix for publication bias.
  • Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail — the web’s long tail will never get clean APIs (economics) and raw HTML can’t substitute for rendering (a large class of answers only exist post-JavaScript); vision-grounded computer-use agents, not API standards, are what reaches it.
  • Reasoning Graphs — a model and a harness are both compression into an executable form; a layered graph of agents (data → reasoning → action) suited to long-horizon, high-consistency processes.
  • Architect Agents — the reasoning graph for each use case is built by an agent, not hand-coded, and the architect agent compounds intelligence at the meta-skill of harness-building.
  • An Open Compute Layer — AI orgs inevitably end up with fragmented, multi-cluster compute; Slurm and Kubernetes are both single-cluster managers; the missing piece is a layer that orchestrates across clusters and lets training/serving dynamically share the same GPU pool.
  • The Origin of Test-Time Compute — reasoning/thinking-time as a third axis alongside subject and difficulty; the first empirical discovery that prompting a model to think before answering raised accuracy, before any model was trained to reason.
  • Interpretability as Scientific Discovery — reverse-engineer superhuman models’ internals to extract genuinely new, human-legible scientific knowledge, rather than only using interpretability for safety or trust.
  • Entropy Collapse — behavioral diversity within an RL training run decays over time; once it collapses, no further improvement is possible regardless of compute, until the recipe itself changes.
  • Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance — decoupling trainer and rollout generation lets a more stable algorithm tolerate more staleness between them, keeping inference engines fully utilized and enabling training across geographically scattered compute.
  • Durable Execution — separating systems concerns (crash recovery) from application logic via a runtime layer; three reasons agentic/LLM workloads are a genuinely new kind of systems problem.
  • Spectrum of Agency — how much autonomy to give an agent is task-dependent; more agency isn’t automatically the better choice.
  • Stateful Visual Encoders — standard visual encoders are invariant to small, meaningful changes by design; a targeted fix makes them change-aware instead.
  • Tactile Reactivity and Multi-Process Architecture — manipulation needs feeling, not just seeing/planning/acting; physical agentic systems need a dual- or multi-process architecture.
  • World Motion Models — predicting geometry/motion rather than pixels when that’s all a task needs; full pixel-level fidelity isn’t always necessary or desirable.
  • Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer — graphs bridge human and machine understanding in a way vectors and model weights don’t; a knowledge layer is active computation, not passive storage; a fourth take on “the data layer built for one purpose isn’t the one agents need.”
  • Market Models — a dedicated model class trained on market dynamics, not text — the same structural move as world models, applied to business decisions; probabilistic “voxels” as its basic unit; “decision regimes” for multi-modal reward landscapes that shift over time.
  • Grounded Capability Delegation — delegate high-stakes quantitative decisions to grounded, purpose-built tools rather than an LLM’s own reasoning; a vanilla agent confused correlation with causation where a capability-grounded agent correctly found genuine demand elasticity.
  • Punk Software — platform dependency is existential risk to your business; a five-part rubric (individual, decentralized, open, anti-monopolistic, moral) for DIY, fully-open AI tooling.
  • Semantic vs. Schema-Rigid Interoperability — protocols requiring identical schemas on both ends vs. protocols relying on intelligence at both endpoints instead; protocol choice should be guided by workload characteristics, not a single default.
  • Visual Imagination in Multimodal Models — models internally reconstruct visual transformations needed to solve spatial-cognition tasks even with no image-generation ability; explicitly supervising this measurably improves performance.
  • An Agent Is a Stack — an agent is model, harness, tools, environment, guardrails, RL system, evaluation infra, and compute; closing any one layer makes the whole ecosystem less portable, competitive, and resilient.
  • RL Environments as the Unstandardized Layer — environments are the mechanism by which capabilities move from domain experts into model weights, and are at the pre-standardization stage model checkpoints were at years ago; OpenEnv’s fix, and a three-way usage taxonomy.
  • Declared vs. Observed Authority — observability and governance aren’t substitutes; a runtime trust plane compares declared agent authority against observed behavior, categorizing drift rather than treating any variance as a binary alarm.
  • Agent Security Taxonomy — three buckets for agent security work: risk assessment, protection (fundamental vs. plug-and-play), and certification/self-improvement.
  • Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming — a red-teaming platform design verified against real system state rather than an LLM judge, with domain-scoped coverage instead of a fixed test count.
  • End-to-End AI Research — a two-years-ago >10-year prediction for end-to-end AI research turned out very wrong; models generate and test thousands of ideas rather than reasoning like a human researcher, inverting “ideas are cheap, execution is everything.”
  • Poison Entry Vectors — a taxonomy of channels (email, calendar invites, images, ultrasonic audio, skills, MCP tool descriptions) through which agent goal-hijacking payloads reach context.
  • Tool Sensitivity and the Lethal Trifecta — blast radius from a hijacked agent scales with connected-tool sensitivity; Willison’s lethal trifecta (untrusted data + sensitive access + external communication) as a simplified risk model.
  • Hallucination-Squatting — LLM hallucination is a supply-chain attack surface: attackers register the exact fictitious artifact names a model confidently recommends, exploiting fast growth, snapshot-learner blindness to deletions, and uneven brand recognition.
  • Zero Ops — remove operations from humans, not humans from operations; “models are not the moat”; outcome-based engineering; a refined maturity model where “full autonomy” means agent-validated outcomes, not unsupervised execution alone.
  • The D3 Framework — “agentic hangover”: more AI use isn’t automatically more productivity; Discover/Plan/Deliver as a disciplined alternative to agent swarms and loop engineering.
  • Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration — routing clinical queries across structured/unstructured data with cost-aware model selection; sub-agents structured around a real clinical protocol (ABCDE) with a synthesizer resolving conflicting outputs.
  • Healthcare AI System Challenges — offline/online evaluation mismatch; recall matters far more in clinical summaries than in typical search; domain knowledge encoded via a semantic knowledge graph.
  • Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents — a mental-health-specific autonomy maturity taxonomy; sandbox/simulation success is not evidence of real-world efficacy; declaring a system’s appropriate severity range rather than overclaiming generality.
  • Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity — an agent’s safety guardrails degrade as task complexity rises; guardrail strength materially affects how an agent doing therapy is perceived.
  • Triple-A Benchmark Standardization — most benchmarks are built around swapping the model, not the full harness; turn benchmarks into agents so both sides integrate through the protocols agents already use to talk to each other.
  • Agents’ Last Exam — agent benchmarks concentrate on programming/math (~7% of real employment); a methodologically serious fix built from an authoritative occupation taxonomy; no single agent wins everywhere.
  • Frontier Cyber Evaluation — four benchmarks spanning the vulnerability lifecycle; evaluation infrastructure is itself part of the attack surface.
  • Verifiable Code Generation — formal verification and LLMs solve each other’s bottleneck; agents close local proof obligations but struggle with repository-wide invariants.
  • Agent 2.0 — minimal scaffolding letting agents spawn sub-agents and write their own tools and memory during execution, rather than pre-specifying topology and tools upfront; validated against a real DEF CON qualifier competition; current models haven’t fully learned to build their own agents yet.
  • Adaptive Agent Frameworks — budget-aware execution as a constrained MDP; parallel reasoning learned during training, not assembled at inference; continual adaptation without catastrophic forgetting.
  • Three-Level Runtime Control — token-level steering via a purpose-built reward model, action control via “genuine self-reflection” that also improves general reasoning, and workflow control via a precomputed, reusable bank rather than a fixed or fully bespoke structure.
  • Small-Model Coding Agent Design — minimize context, take tiny verified steps, and reserve reasoning for recovery loops; small models still specifically struggle to verify their own work.
  • Agent Memory Lifecycle — ingest/consolidate/forget/retrieve/reconsolidate; consolidation cadence is domain-dependent, not temporal; “logs are not memories.”
  • Memory Evaluation Framework — retention, retrieval, and task-completion as three increasingly realistic, expensive, and important evaluation tiers for agent memory systems.
  • Verifiable Substrate — a three-part definition of what makes AI-driven scientific discovery verifiable: grounded idea generation, mutation on top of verified reproductions, and claims that trace to real logs, code, or hardware runs.
  • Intent Loops — harnessing tacit expertise (why experts act, not just what they do) so agentic automation sustains human participation through traceable attribution rather than squeezing humans out.
  • Sidewalk Autonomy — sidewalk robots face a distinct, socially denser and more resource-constrained autonomy problem than road vehicles; simulation built from real video closes the sim-to-real gap.
  • Digital Twins vs. Digital Cousins — video reconstruction gives one environment per video (a digital twin); scene-graph-based object swapping generates multiple variations (digital cousins) from a single capture.
  • Simulation Evolution for Physical AI — three stages of robotics simulation: artist-built graphics, reconstruction (NeRF/Gaussian splats, bounded by what was captured), and generative world models (fully data-driven, can hallucinate uncaptured scenarios).
  • Interactive World Model Architecture — the technical recipe for real-time, action-conditioned generative world models: base video model, domain post-training, causal architecture, distillation for speed.
  • Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel — harness capability (information, execution, feedback) gets distilled permanently into model weights via training, generation over generation; a counterpoint on a different time horizon to harness-as-moat.
  • Orchard and UltraEnv — container-native environment-execution infrastructure (UltraEnv) and orchestration (Orchard) for running many agents against many environments at scale.
  • Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning — EvolveLab: agents improving across attempts by distilling lessons from experience rather than replaying raw traces.
  • Sandbox Infrastructure for RL Rollouts — trainer/rollout-generator/sandbox decomposition for RL, illustrated with a Qwen3-8B case study; RL taught harness-compliance, not new reasoning.
  • Harness Diversity as Data Augmentation — Kimi K3 randomizes harness features during training for robustness, versus Cursor Composer 2’s opposite bet to specialize to one harness.
  • On-Policy Distillation of Expert RL Models — Kimi K3’s final model is nine reasoning-level × domain expert models distilled into one via on-policy distillation.
  • Train-Inference Mismatch — divergence between an RL rollout engine and training engine silently degrades training from on-policy toward off-policy; fixes span kernels to algorithms.
  • Inference Engine Design for Agentic Serving — agentic workloads shift serving priorities toward cache reuse and disaggregation, away from single-turn-chat throughput optimization.
  • Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability — five named barriers (invisible errors, soft prompt control, the metacognition gap, non-verifiable RL, cost) explaining why reliability lags other axes of intelligence.
  • Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic — randomizing the orchestrator/model in live agentic sessions to measure treatment effects, rather than scoring against a static benchmark.
  • Meta-Harness Architecture — a server/runner orchestration layer above existing harnesses, giving composition, collaboration, and session-level control without absorbing harnesses into the model.
  • Runtime Agent Optimization — continuously optimizing an agent’s model/harness/execution- strategy configuration against a Pareto frontier of cost, quality, and latency.
  • Principles for Durable Benchmarks — research-agenda thesis, roadmap-setting, researcher UX, task quality, difficulty/headroom, and rigorous QC, versus “bench slop” and benchmark gaming.
  • Taste as a Benchmark Metric — Senior SWE-Bench’s “tasteful solve”: codebase and practice alignment scored explicitly, beyond raw correctness.
  • Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) — evaluating an agent as a system across business outcomes, task success, component evaluation, and diagnostics; evals as the durable asset.
  • Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery — keeping an agent entirely off the numerical- computation path so fidelity is guaranteed by construction, not evaluation.
  • Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability — a four-category failure taxonomy and measured tool/ knowledge-architecture fixes (setup vs. discretionary tools, a diagnostic-playbook structure).
  • Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck — long horizon and sparse reward combine into a bottleneck needing many-x, not incremental, improvement; illustrated via open math-research problems.
  • Reward Stack Replaces Data Stack — reward/environment design as the field’s new scarce, defining resource, replacing data curation’s role in the pretraining era.
  • Semantic Alignment for Cross-Modal Translation — a contrastive training recipe letting a 1,000x-smaller model beat frontier models on auto-formalization and code translation.
  • Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks — capability benchmarks and enterprise deployment-readiness needs are structurally opposed; the path to improvement is economic (reducing oversight cost), not a rising score.
  • The Good Regulator Theorem and Agentic Debt — a 1970 cybernetics theorem explaining why delegating authority to a poorly-modeled system is structurally unsafe; the resulting failure mode named “agentic debt.”
  • Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice — multi-agent orchestration reframed as a runtime delegation decision with multi-valued ground truth, distinct from bounded tool selection because agent delegation can start an unbounded, never-returning loop.
  • The Software Factory — the implicit signal-to-deployed-software loop every software company runs; model independence, sovereignty, full org scope, and a shared agent core as design principles.
  • Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy — agent autonomy is gated by deterministic, verifiable feedback in the environment, not model capability alone; a fifth instance of the wiki’s environments-as-bottleneck theme.
  • Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories — governance as a platform responsibility, guardrails scaled to the org size you’re growing into, and outcome metrics over token counts.
  • Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks — Neuro SAN: JSON-described agents/tools, a credential side-channel, agentic webs, agent-generated agent networks, and a 200-leaf-agent production deployment.
  • Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks — single-API-task scores of 88-97% collapse to 44-73% once chained, from step dependency alone; a three-gate methodology for trustworthy synthetic benchmark tasks.
  • Production Agent Case Studies at NVIDIA — measured results from a bug-fixing autobot, a new-model bring-up pipeline, and a training-optimization agent on TensorRT-LLM.
  • Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs — probabilistic agent intelligence, lightweight harnesses, and two counter-intuitive findings: full autonomy and centralization aren’t always better.
  • Physics-Bounded Compute Escalation — a biological power ceiling for wearables and a three-tier escalation model: escalate compute only when the task actually calls for it.
  • Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops — a planner/executor architecture for hardware optimization, plus four portable lessons on reward hacking, visibility scope, rule hygiene, and knowledge-base pruning.
  • Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness — removing the external verifier from scientific-discovery evolution entirely, using token log-probabilities and diversity as fitness instead.
  • Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents — three infra shifts (UX, compute, trust), a harness-code architecture with code-defined evaluators, and a warm-pool control plane for agent-scale job launching.
  • Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery — knowledge, measurement, simulation, and physical experimentation as what AI needs to automate discovery; a self-targeted RSI result that may update Vinyals’ “hasn’t happened yet” claim.
  • Policy-Checking Evaluator Agent — Capital One’s four-role architecture (understanding/ planner/evaluator/explainer) with an explicit reject-and-loop-back path; contrasted with Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery as two different answers to high-stakes agent reliability.
  • Agent-Native Payment Rails — three structural reasons agents need a different payment substrate than humans (programmability, finality, privacy-vs-auditability), plus an open- architecture fix and a live micropayment marketplace for agent-to-agent task commerce.
  • Neurosymbolic AI — a probabilistic LLM wired to a formal symbolic layer; hallucination as the feature you fence rather than fix, the Aristotle→Gruber and 1956→agents lineages, and why symbolic AI returns as a checking layer rather than as the whole system.
  • Ontology as Agent Guardrail — an ontology-backed reasoner inside the tool-use loop: “Pydantic at the door, ontology at the ledger”, side-effect-free agents, the RDFS/OWL constructs that do the checking, and three error classes free text can’t catch.
